text:
The fog had been rolling in off the North Sea for three days, thick enough to taste like salt and iron. Elias Thorne, the lighthouse keeper of Gull’s Point, had grown accustomed to the isolation, but the silence of the storm was different. It wasn’t the roaring absence of wind; it was a heavy, pressurized quiet that made his ears pop.

Elias climbed the one hundred and twelve steps of the spiral staircase, his joints protesting with every turn. At the top, in the lantern room, he wiped the condensation from the glass. The great Fresnel lens, a cathedral of glass and brass, sat dark. The automated system had been handling the light for the last decade, but Elias still checked it every hour. It was a ritual, a prayer to the sea.

That was when he saw it.

It wasn’t a ship. Ships left wakes, or at least the faintest disturbance in the water. This was a point of light, hovering just above the surface of the churning black water, three miles out. It pulsed. Not the steady, rhythmic flash of a navigation beacon, but a complex, staccato rhythm. *Click-click-pause-click-click-click.*
